mūla.iast: prakṛtiṃ puruṣaṃ caiva viddhy anādī ubhāv api | vikārāṃś ca guṇāṃś caiva viddhi prakṛti-saṃbhavān

advaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
advaita.divergence_note: Śaṅkara (source 13.20) makes the pair the Lord's two powers rather than two independent reals, and spends his argument refuting a rival tatpuruṣa parsing (na ādī) of anādī; prakṛti is explicitly identified with triguṇa māyā. Guṇa are read as the pleasure-pain-delusion forms of cognition, not as ethical virtues (contrast Rāmānuja).
advaita.english_rendering: Know prakṛti (matter-nature) and puruṣa (the conscious principle) as the two prakṛti of Īśvara (the Lord), both anādi (without beginning): since the Lord is eternal, His two natures must be eternal too, and to possess these two is precisely what makes Him Lord. Those who split anādī as 'not the first' so as to keep the Lord as sole cause are wrong, for before the two arose there would be nothing to rule, and saṃsāra (the round of birth), bondage and release would become causeless and scripture pointless. Know the vikāra (modifications), from buddhi (intellect) down to body and senses, and the guṇa (qualities) that turn into pleasure, pain and delusion, as born of prakṛti, which is the Lord's triguṇa māyā (three-stranded power of manifestation).

viśiṣṭādvaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
viśiṣṭādvaita.english_rendering: Know that prakṛti (matter) and puruṣa (the self), mutually conjoined, are both anādi (beginningless). And know that both the vikāra (modifications) such as desire and aversion, which cause bondage, and the guṇa (qualities) such as amānitva (freedom from pride) and the rest, which cause release, are born of prakṛti. This same prakṛti, joined to the self from time without beginning and transformed into the form of the kṣetra (field, the body), binds the self through desire and aversion, and that very prakṛti, through humility and the other virtues, becomes the cause of its apavarga (liberation).
viśiṣṭādvaita.divergence_note: Rāmānuja (source 13.19) reads vikāra as the passions (icchā-dveṣa) and, strikingly, guṇa as the virtues listed at 13.7-11 (amānitva etc.), so the half-verse becomes a statement that one and the same prakṛti supplies both the chains and the means of release. No school but Vallabha (who follows him) takes guṇa this way; for Śaṅkara, Śrīdhara and Madhusūdana guṇa are the pleasure-pain-delusion modes.

dvaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
dvaita.divergence_note: Read with Jayatīrtha's Prameyadīpikā on Madhva's bhāṣya (their 13.20): Madhva frames the verse as preparing for 'from what, what' (13.4), says the guṇa (qualities) are sattva (clarity) and the rest, and explains that the vikāra (modifications) are listed separately because the guṇa differ from them only very slightly in passing from laya (dissolution) to sarga (creation), citing a Mādhucchandasa text that calls the three both effect and not effect. Jayatīrtha adds the doctrinally weighty points. He reads 'from what, what' as the nature of the preraka (impeller), and argues that describing the impeller needs prior knowledge of the prerya (what is impelled), which is the field with its kinds; hence it is summed up here, not earlier, which would have been prolix. He states that everything other than Īśvara (the Lord), conscious and non-conscious, is called kṣetra (field); that prakṛti (primal matter) here means the twenty-four principles listed from the great elements on; that vikāra covers all modifications, the three guṇa included, set apart only by a particular intention; and that puruṣa here means the jīva (individual self). He also says the sum is brief because the theme returns at 13.26, and rejects the reading of guṇa as pleasure, pain and delusion (marked in the edition as Śaṅkara), since those are already among the modifications and listing them again would be improper. Neither commentator glosses anādi (beginningless), which is rendered as the verse says. The others differ sharply: Advaita and Advaita-bhakti read the guṇa as pleasure, pain and delusion, the reading Jayatīrtha rejects; Viśiṣṭādvaita takes the guṇa as the virtues that lead to release; Śuddhādvaita and Bhakti make prakṛti the power and the puruṣa a portion of the Lord. Dvaita places the jīva inside the field and the Lord outside it as its impeller.
dvaita.english_rendering: Know prakṛti (primal matter) and puruṣa, here the jīva (individual self), as both beginningless, and know the vikāra (modifications) and the guṇa (qualities), sattva (clarity) and the rest, as born of prakṛti. Everything other than Īśvara (the Lord), conscious and non-conscious alike, is the kṣetra (field), and it is summed up here because the next topic is the One who impels it, and the impeller cannot be described until what He impels is known. The guṇa are named apart from the vikāra, though they too arise from prakṛti, because they are both effect and not effect, their arising out of dissolution into creation being very slight, as the Mādhucchandasa recension says.

śuddhādvaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
śuddhādvaita.english_rendering: This is the Bhagavat's own sāṅkhya (enumeration of principles), not that of the sāṅkhya partisans for whom prakṛti is an eternal second beside the self: here prakṛti is the Lord's śakti (power), in two forms, as effect the upādhi (limiting adjunct) of the jīva (individual self) bound with avidyā (ignorance), and as cause the māyā of the paramātman (supreme self); likewise puruṣa is the aṃśin (whole), the root person, and the jīva are His aṃśa (portions). By līlā (play), by His own will, He took up prakṛti; know both as My aṃśa, sat-cit (being-consciousness) in nature, anādi because not other than their cause. Know the vikāra, desire and aversion that bind, and the guṇa, humility and the rest, or sattva and the rest, that lead to amṛta (immortality), as born of prakṛti.
śuddhādvaita.divergence_note: Vallabha (source 13.20) repositions the whole verse inside a 'Bhagavadīya sāṅkhya' and doubles each term: prakṛti as effect (jīva's adjunct) and as cause (the Lord's māyā), puruṣa as root-whole and as portions. Beginninglessness comes from non-difference from the cause, not from independent eternity, and the taking-up of prakṛti is līlā (Bhāgavata 3.26.4-5). He keeps Rāmānuja's virtue-reading of guṇa but offers sattva etc. as an alternative.

bhakti.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
bhakti.divergence_note: Śrīdhara (source 13.20) gives a regress (anavasthā) argument for beginninglessness and grounds it devotionally: prakṛti as the Lord's power, puruṣa as His portion. He explicitly defers to Śaṅkara's bhāṣya for the full proof, so his divergence from Advaita here is in the aṃśa language, not in a rival argument.
bhakti.english_rendering: With this verse and the next four the Lord expounds 'what its modifications are and from what it comes, who he is and what his power', by declaring prakṛti and puruṣa the causes of saṃsāra (the round of birth). Know both as anādi (beginningless), for if they had a beginning, another prakṛti would be needed for them, and so without end; prakṛti is beginningless as the śakti (power) of the beginningless Īśvara, and puruṣa is beginningless as His aṃśa (portion), a point Śaṅkara has argued at length, so I do not expand it. Know the vikāra, body, senses and the rest, and the guṇa, their transformations as pleasure, pain and delusion, as sprung from prakṛti.

advaita-bhakti.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
advaita-bhakti.divergence_note: Madhusūdana (source 13.20) harmonizes the verse with 7.4-6 (aparā and parā prakṛti) and gives two separate proofs of beginninglessness: regress for prakṛti, the karmic argument (kṛtahāni-akṛtābhyāgama) for puruṣa. His vikāra are the classical sixteen, a narrower count than Śaṅkara's 'buddhi down to body and senses'.
advaita-bhakti.english_rendering: In the seventh chapter the Lord set out His two prakṛti, the lower, which is the kṣetra (field), and the higher, which is the jīva (living being); here the lower is called prakṛti, the three-stranded māyā, the power of the Supreme Lord, and the higher is called puruṣa, so there is no contradiction. Know both as anādi (without a cause): prakṛti because it is the cause of the whole world and to seek a cause for it would be endless regress; puruṣa because the joy, grief and fear of every newborn are driven by its past dharma and adharma (merit and demerit), else one would suffer the unearned and lose the earned. Know the vikāra, the sixteen (five great elements and eleven senses), and the guṇa, sattva, rajas and tamas as pleasure, pain and delusion, as having prakṛti alone for their cause.

vishishtadvaita.divergence_note: Unlike Advaita, Vishishtadvaita keeps prakrti as a real eternal body of Ishvara, not maya; the jiva-purusa is a real individual spirit, never identical to Brahman, only inseparably related as attribute to substance.

shuddhadvaita.divergence_note: Shuddhadvaita alone reads the verse as affirming that both poles emerge FROM Brahman (not alongside Brahman); liberation is not escape from prakrti but enjoyment of Krsna's own being through His grace-gift (pushti).

so_what_questions: If the raw material of my temperament had no starting point, am I responsible for it or only for what I do with it?
Are my worst reactions and my best habits made of the same stuff, and if so, does that change how I work on them?
When I say 'I am anxious' or 'I am confident', which part of me is actually doing the feeling?
Is it possible to stop asking 'when did this pattern start?' and still change it?
If my body, moods and abilities are all products of one underlying nature, what is left that I can call me?
Should I treat my team's personalities as fixed givens, or as material that can be reshaped?

everyday_applications.advaita: When you catch yourself saying 'I am a stressed person', notice that the stress, the body and even the clever mind analysing it are all listed here as products of one power, none of them the knower. A manager can stop trying to fix a team's moods by argument and start by refusing to treat any mood, including their own, as who they are.
everyday_applications.viśiṣṭādvaita: The same material that produces your envy at a colleague's promotion can produce your humility; Rāmānuja says one nature makes both. So the practical work is not escaping your nature but redirecting it: the energy of a resentful afternoon can be turned, deliberately, into the patience and modesty that actually free you.
everyday_applications.dvaita: Before you work out who is really steering an organization, map everything that is being steered, and put yourself and the other people on that map along with the machinery. A consultant who leaves themselves off the chart will misread who is moving whom, and it also pays to keep near-identical categories apart, such as a company's basic culture and the particular habits it has produced, rather than letting one stand in for the other.
everyday_applications.śuddhādvaita: Vallabha would have a parent see both the child and the messy circumstances of the child's life as portions of the same source, taken up in play rather than as a punishment. That reframes a chaotic household not as a problem to be solved before joy is allowed, but as the field where the play is already happening.
everyday_applications.bhakti: Śrīdhara's regress argument is useful when you get stuck asking 'but what caused that?' about a family conflict or an organisational mess: at some point the chain has no first link, and the only useful question is how you act now. He then leaves the long proofs to someone else, a good model for a teacher who knows when to point to the textbook.
everyday_applications.advaita-bhakti: Madhusūdana's karmic argument says a newborn's fear and joy are not random; they carry history. A founder inheriting a company's culture can use this: the reactions people bring on day one have causes older than you, so diagnose before you blame, and do not expect a new policy to erase what came before it.

primary_meaning: Know that *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* are both without beginning, and that every modification of the field, together with the three *guṇas*, is born of *prakṛti* alone.
